exact_claim: Stubbins Ffirth was a medical student at the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia; he defended his thesis on 6 June 1804 for the degree of Doctor of Medicine
primary_source: P1 Ffirth 1804 title leaf + inner title
visual_rights: Title page public domain (NLM / Wellcome scan)
notes: Say 'a medical student in Philadelphia'. During the experiments (1802-03) he was a student, not yet a doctor; the title 'The Doctor Who…' is a stretch (he became an M.D. in 1804)

exact_claim: Thesis title: 'A Treatise on Malignant Fever; with an Attempt to Prove its Non-Contagious Nature' (Philadelphia: printed for the author by B. Graves, 1804); the inner title adds 'from Reason, Observation, and Experiment'
notes: 'Malignant fever' = yellow fever in his usage. On-screen title card can show the real title page

exact_claim: Title as given in the slate: '…with an Attempt to Prove its Non-contagious Non-malignant Nature'
notes: The words 'Non-malignant' are not in the title. Use the real title (C02)

exact_claim: Title page: 'A native of Salem, New Jersey'; 'House Surgeon of the Philadelphia Dispensary'
notes: Optional colour: 'a young man from Salem, New Jersey'

exact_claim: Born c. 1781-82: his gravestone says he died 4 July 1820 'in the Thirty-Ninth year of his age' (aged 38), so he was about 20 when the experiments began in Oct 1802
notes: Say 'about 20' or 'barely 20', never an exact birth date. Do not say 1784

exact_claim: The self-experiments ran during the Philadelphia yellow fever epidemics of 1802 and 1803; the first is dated 4 October 1802; the thesis was published in 1804
notes: Say 'Philadelphia, 1802'. Do not say the experiments were in 1804 (that is the thesis year)

exact_claim: When he first saw the fever in the city he believed it was contagious and imported; later facts and his experiments convinced him it 'never was, and unless the laws of nature should change, never will be a contagious disease'
notes: Good arc beat: 'He started out believing it was catching… then changed his mind'

exact_claim: He worked at the city hospital during the 1802 epidemic ('my situation at the city hospital in the year 1802') and saw patients in the city in 1802 and 1803
notes: Do not name or locate the hospital building (not confirmed)

exact_claim: His motive: fear made families abandon the sick ('the wife shuns the chamber of her husband, the husband of his wife, children of their parents…'); he believed proving non-contagion would cut deaths by half; quarantine was also ruining trade
notes: Stakes line. Do NOT quote the rest of the p.46 passage: it contains a racist slur about Black nurses

exact_claim: Animals first: a small dog was fed bread soaked in black vomit, then the vomit alone for a week; a cat was given 3 ounces a day for 5 days; both stayed healthy
visual_rights: Describe, never show; no animal eating vomit on screen
notes: Optional one line: 'He tried it on a dog and a cat first. Nothing.'

exact_claim: He injected an ounce of black vomit into a dog's jugular vein and the dog died in ten minutes; he repeated it with plain water and got 'precisely the same result', so he blamed the injection, not the vomit
notes: A real control experiment, but a dead dog. Best left out of a Short

exact_claim: 4 Oct 1802: he cut his left forearm (between elbow and wrist) enough to draw a few drops of blood and put fresh black vomit into the cut; slight inflammation, gone in 3 days
visual_rights: Describe; show a bandaged arm / lancet only
notes: 'He cut his arm and rubbed it in.' Keep it clean: no wound close-up

exact_claim: Four days later: a bigger cut in his right arm, five drops of fresh black vomit, closed with plaster and bandage for two days; healed without pus
He repeated the cut experiments 'above twenty times on various parts of my body' during both the 1802 and 1803 epidemics
notes: 'More than twenty times.'

exact_claim: Two drops of fresh black vomit in his right eye: it 'felt a little uneasy for about a minute' but no pain or inflammation
visual_rights: Show a dropper and a squint, never the liquid in the eye
notes: 'Two drops… in his eye.' Mild symptom: a minute of discomfort

exact_claim: He heated 3 ounces of black vomit in an iron skillet over the fire and held his head over it, breathing the steam, with no unpleasant effect
visual_rights: Skillet + steam only; contents never visible
notes: Say 'heated it in a skillet and breathed the fumes'. 'Fried' is a retelling word

exact_claim: Next he sat two hours in a small room heated to 100°F while 6 ounces evaporated, often holding his head over the dish; he got a great headache, nausea, heavy sweating, faintness and chest tightness, which passed in fresh air; he blamed the heat, not the vomit
notes: His only real symptoms. Phrase: 'He felt awful… and blamed the heat.'

exact_claim: He rolled the dried residue from that experiment into pills and swallowed them all the same day, 'without the least effect'
visual_rights: Pills on a saucer are fine to show
notes: Strong visual escalation step

exact_claim: He drank half an ounce of black vomit, fresh from a patient, diluted in an ounce and a half of water: taste 'very slightly acid', pulse 76 and unchanged, 'no more effect was produced than if I had taken water alone'
visual_rights: A cup only; never show contents or the act of drinking in close-up
notes: 'Drank it' is accurate. Half an ounce ≈ 15 ml

exact_claim: Over two epidemics he repeated these 'a great number of times' and raised the dose from half an ounce to two ounces, 'drinking it at length without dilution'
notes: Climax line: 'In the end, two ounces. Undiluted.' Two ounces ≈ 60 ml (about a quarter cup); say 'two ounces'

exact_claim: He then tested other fluids: serum from the blood of a patient in the first (early) stage, four drops in a cut in his left leg and also swallowed; saliva from a dying patient by lancet puncture and in cuts; then sweat and bile; urine gave some inflammation; all healed
notes: Say 'blood serum, saliva, sweat… even urine'. Not 'he injected/transfused blood'

exact_claim: He slept 'several times all night on a bed where a patient lay extremely ill… with black vomit' and made it a practice to take patients' breath in his face
notes: Usable cold-open image: a student sleeping beside a fever patient

exact_claim: He never fell ill from any of it
notes: Exception to state honestly if asked: headache/nausea in the 100°F room (C17), brief eye discomfort, small inflammations

exact_claim: Conclusion: 'I hold it, therefore, as a fact, that malignant fever is not a contagious disease; that it never has been, and from the established laws of nature stamped on it, never can be'
visual_rights: Quote can sit over the title page
notes: Quotable. Shorter version: 'It never has been [contagious], and… never can be.' Page from the NLM scan (check against the page image before printing p.59)

exact_claim: After drinking: 'how is it possible that I should never have the least effect produced?'
notes: Optional voice line; shows his confidence

exact_claim: In his own description black vomit belongs to the third and final stage, 'one from which very few recover'; one sample came from a patient 'in the last agonies which precede dissolution', saliva from a patient 'in the last stage'
notes: Supports 'the samples came from the dying'. Black vomit = blood digested in the stomach (for us: 'black vomit', no further detail)

exact_claim: Why he never got sick: yellow fever spreads through the bite of an infected mosquito (mainly Aedes), not by touching, breathing or swallowing patients' fluids
source_2: S7 PBS American Experience (Reed fomite test)
notes: Core twist: 'He wasn't catching it… because the disease needed a mosquito.' Avoid saying vomit 'can never' transmit anything

exact_claim: His black-vomit samples came from late-stage patients whose blood probably no longer carried much virus (the virus peaks just before the fever and in the first 3-5 days)
notes: Say 'probably' / 'by then the virus had mostly gone'. Secondary reason only; the mosquito is the main reason. Wikipedia states it flatly: do not copy that

exact_claim: One sample WAS early-stage: blood serum from a patient 'in the first or inflammatory stage', put into a leg cut. Why that did not infect him is not explained by any source found
notes: Do not explain it (no source). Do not claim he was immune from an earlier infection (no source). Keep out of the script

exact_claim: Finlay proposed the mosquito in Havana in 1881; the US Army commission under Walter Reed confirmed it in Cuba in 1900
source_1: HCS07 research (P1 Finlay 1881; P2 Reed reports)
notes: Callback to the Finlay Short (Dec 3). 1881 is 61 years after Ffirth died: 'sixty years after his death'

exact_claim: From 30 Nov 1900, three volunteers of Reed's team slept twenty nights in a hut full of bedding and clothing soiled by yellow fever patients; none got yellow fever
notes: Bookend twist: 'A century later, the Army tried it too…' One line max

exact_claim: Reed's team also showed that injected blood from a patient could pass the disease on
source_1: Reed Carroll Agramonte JAMA 1901;36:431-440 (seen only in summary)
notes: Not checked in the original. Not needed for the Short

exact_claim: 'He was right: yellow fever is not contagious'
notes: Right that it doesn't pass by contact; wrong that it doesn't pass from person to person (it does, via the mosquito) and wrong about the cause: he blamed heat, filth, putrefaction and bad air. Phrase: 'right for the wrong reason' or 'half right'

exact_claim: He saw that cold weather stopped the fever and that it never became epidemic below 32°F, and used this as proof it was not contagious
notes: Ironic but only voice the irony (frost kills the mosquitoes) if a source is added; none checked yet
